name: Ward Mrozek
languages: Polish (from his grandmother, and the polka station out of Pulaski)
equipment: Leather jacket: brown, cracked, with a Teamsters local patch and POLECAT stitched over the pocket
Pump shotgun: a 12-gauge he keeps behind the seat for nothing in particular, five in the tube
Tool kit, a big one, and a creeper
Work clothes, coveralls and leather gloves
A rag that is never clean
CB radio: a forty-channel set in the cab with a big whip antenna, and a hand-held walkie-talkie
A thermos, a carton of Pall Malls, a log book two days behind
A photograph of his daughter Kasia, nine, in Kenosha, tucked in the sun visor
Truck: a 1971 Kenworth cabover named Gloria, with a forty-foot refrigerated trailer of Wisconsin cheese he is supposed to have in Minneapolis by Monday
features: Up Before Dawn (Farm-Raised origin: he needs only 6 hours for a long rest and can't be surprised while awake in the last hour before sunrise; advantage on saving throws against exhaustion from hard work, cold and lost sleep; he notices without a check when animals are frightened, sick or behaving wrongly, and what that usually means)

Hard to Kill (Roughneck: once per long rest, when reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 instead; he ignores his first level of exhaustion and has advantage on CON saving throws against exhaustion, cold and hard labor)

Heavy Work (Roughneck: advantage on STR checks to lift, push, pull, break or force something; he counts as one size larger for what he can carry, drag or lift, and he can carry an unconscious adult at his full speed)

Bull-Headed (Roughneck, 2nd level: once per short rest, when he fails a fear check, he turns it to anger: he gains no Dread, but on his next turn must move toward the source and attack it or break whatever stands between him and it; if he can't reach it, he smashes something nearby)
Trade: Teamster (Roughneck, 3rd level: he is already proficient in Driving, and has advantage on Driving checks to keep a vehicle on the road or get a stalled one started under pressure)

Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: in any town he can find work at the garage or the elevator, and mechanics and drivers talk to him as one of their own; given a few minutes with a vehicle, generator or engine, he can tell what is wrong with it without a check, including whether someone made it go wrong)

personality.traits: I talk to my truck, my radio and strangers, in that order. I fix things that aren't mine. I would rather drive all night than sleep in a motel.
personality.ideals: You give a kid a ride, you see her to the door. My dad said that about girls on the road and he was right.
personality.bonds: My daughter Kasia in Kenosha, who I see every other Sunday. Gloria the Kenworth. And a girl called Dawn who rode with me from the Beloit truck stop to Hollow Fork, smoked my Pall Malls when she ran out of Kools, sang along to Merle Haggard badly, and asked me to let her out at that little town with the pretty elevator because she liked the look of it.
personality.flaws: I let her out. I had a slice of pie, I waved, and I drove away. I have a temper, and right now most of it is pointed at myself.

appearance: Thirty-seven, big, thick-necked and soft-spoken, with a brown beard, a Brewers cap, forearms like a blacksmith's and a road-map of grease in the creases of his hands.
backstory: Wladyslaw Mrozek, Ward since second grade, grew up on a forty-cow dairy farm outside Pulaski, Wisconsin, milking before school, until his father sold out in 1959 and moved the family to Kenosha to work at the car plant. Ward hated the plant, learned diesels in the Army in Germany, and has driven over the road since 1962: cheese and butter out of the Wisconsin co-ops to Chicago, the Twin Cities, Des Moines. Divorced, one daughter. His handle is Polecat because of a story about a skunk and a sleeper cab that he will tell anyone who asks. On Thursday 29 August he picked up a hitchhiker called Dawn at the truck stop by Beloit, heading for Minneapolis, and took Highway 14 west because he had a drop in La Crosse; at Hollow Fork she asked him to stop, because of the elevator and the banner and the green corn, and he bought her a slice of pie at the Fork Diner and drove on. On Friday 20 September a nurse from Rockford found him on the CB at the same truck stop, holding a postcard that said 'Tell Polecat thanks for the ride.' He left his trailer of cheese at a reefer yard in Madison and drove north. (Hook: the hitchhiker who called home. He has eaten the town's pie, once, and the town will be glad to see him again. His CB and his rig are the party's best tools in hs-scenario-003.)
